papers.title: Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling: Brain and Cardiac Effective Connectivity
papers.abstract: Brain-body interactions underpin embodied inference and interoception, and are central to both general health and the pathophysiology of mental health disorders. These interactions are orchestrated across a hierarchy extending from the cortex, through the brainstem, to peripheral autonomic effectors. Existing methods either reduce this communication to scalar summaries or lack an invertible biophysical model, and so cannot resolve where in this extended architecture an observed effect originates. To address this, we introduce Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling, an extension of the generative causal modelling framework that formalises hierarchical message passing across the full brain-body axis. We instantiate the framework for brain-heart interactions with the Brainstem Cardiac Network, a closed-loop neural mass model of brainstem autonomic circuitry and sinoatrial node dynamics. By incorporating five brainstem nuclei, a viscerosensory thalamic relay and the cardiac pacemaker, the network enables estimation of directed effective connectivity across the cortical-brainstem-cardiac axis. As an illustrative case study, representative of the experiments and extended physiological systems that Embodied DCM and the BCN can now interrogate, we applied the framework to simultaneously recorded electroencephalography and electrocardiography during an auditory Go/No-Go paradigm. A multimodal observation model permits joint inversion of electrophysiological and cardiac responses, so that neural and bodily measurements together constrain an account of central and peripheral dynamics. The case study shows how the framework can arbitrate between competing hypotheses about functional cytoarchitecture, distinguishing granular from agranular microcircuits within the viscero-sensorimotor hierarchy. It also shows how time-varying estimates of synaptic efficacy can be recovered alongside continuous latent neuronal dynamics, over extended windows spanning anticipation, target processing and motor inhibition. By linking neural and cardiac signals to a single generative architecture, this work moves the study of brain-heart interactions beyond correlation, providing a framework for testing theories of embodied inference and for identifying circuit-level disruptions in disorders of interoceptive and autonomic regulation.

papers.title: Sensory representation by non-equilibrium flows of neural activity at the mesoscale of cortex
papers.abstract: We present a non-equilibrium theory of sensory perception and the mesoscale of sensory cortex. We propose that local neuron assemblies (cortical columns) toggle spontaneously between activity states (on and off) and that small populations of columns are coupled within and between areas of sensory cortex. The resulting network generates sudden, large-scale fluctuations and represents sensory inputs and perceptions by characteristic patterns of activity flows. The non-equilibrium dynamic is governed by the variational principle of maximal path entropy, or Maximum Caliber. Many current theories, by contrast, posit equilibrium dynamics and representation with activity states Our minimal model of sensory cortex describes populations of columns from two cortical areas and is fully constrained by empirical observations of `reversals' in perceived appearance, which occur spontaneously for visual, auditory, and tactile stimulation. We formalize representation by activity flows with dynamic Hamiltonian functions. Surprisingly, effective representation requires small-number fluctuations of toggling columns, as larger numbers would be dominated by hysteresis. Finally, we detail predictions for the microscale of spiking neurons that follow from on-off toggling and non-equilibrium dynamics. We conclude that the neural levels underlying perception are functionally organized in terms of activity flows. The inherent instability of non-equilibrium ensures active updating and renders all perceptions open to immediate revision. We conjecture that current theories of brain function (such as the Free Energy Principle) could be reformulated in terms of the variational principle of non-equilibrium, Maximum Caliber.

papers.title: CD40 ligand and IFN-γ induce proinflammatory activity and microglia-mediated neurodegeneration in human stem cell models
papers.abstract: The cluster of differentiation 40 (CD40)/CD40 ligand (CD40L) co-stimulatory pathway plays a critical role in the activation and regulation of immune networks involving both adaptive and innate immune cells. Dysregulation of this pathway has been implicated in multiple autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration driven by compartmentalized neuroinflammation within the central nervous system (CNS), sustained low-grade T cell infiltration at the blood-brain barrier, and T cell reactivation at CNS border tissues. CD40L-expressing T cells can activate CD40-expressing microglia, which are a critical effector cell that contribute to neurodegeneration in MS. However, the consequence of this functional interaction in the brain remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the combination of CD40L and interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}), a cytokine produced by activated T cells, induces a robust inflammatory response and cell death in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC)-derived microglia. Stimulation with CD40L elicited microglial clustering, morphological transformation, and robust release of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-12 (IL-12), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-), and IL-6. Anti-CD40L antibody treatment reversed both cell death and inflammatory response and partially normalized the associated transcriptional changes. Furthermore, using an hiPSC-derived tri-culture system comprising neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, we demonstrated that CD40L and IFN-{gamma} trigger microglia-dependent neuronal dysregulation and death. Anti-CD40L treatment substantially attenuated neuronal injury. Finally, transcriptomic enrichment analysis identified CD40L-mediated microglial gene expression signatures that correlated with CD40 expression in primary progressive MS brain tissue but not in the normal-appearing white matter of healthy controls. Collectively, these findings support a role for the microglial CD40/T cell CD40L axis in MS pathology and suggest CD40L blockade as a potential therapeutic strategy warranting further investigation.

papers.title: Electroencephalographic activity patterns distinguish interdigitated default and frontoparietal networks
papers.abstract: The brain is comprised of distributed functional networks that operate on diverse time scales. Evidence from precision fMRI shows that canonical networks, including default (DN), frontoparietal control (FPCN), and dorsal attention (dATN), each fractionate into multiple finely interdigitated networks. However, as fMRI is blind to fast processes underlying neural communication, there remains a need to neurophysiologically characterize individual-level network fractionation. To address this need, we conducted a simultaneous EEG-fMRI study, including multiple sessions per individual, resting-state and task conditions, and carbon wire loop sensors for optimized artifact correction. Using precision network mapping, we discovered dissociable electrophysiological correlates of blood-oxygen-level-dependent activity for two networks within the boundaries of the canonical DN. One (DNa) related more positively with alpha and high-beta power, while another (DNb) related more negatively with theta and low-beta power. Univariate and machine learning analyses further revealed electrophysiological dissociations between networks within the canonical FPCN (FPCNa versus FPCNb) but not dATN. The network-specific electrophysiological activity patterns were reliable across sessions, only modestly variable between resting-state and demanding task conditions, and observable for neighboring nodes of different networks across multiple cortical zones. Our findings provide insight into rhythmic neural processes that fine-grained networks may engage to support divergent cognitive operations.

papers.title: The anti-dyskinetic and the anti-parkinsonian effects of sub-anesthetic ketamine are also present in female preclinical models
papers.abstract: Biological sex is an important determinant of neuropharmacological response, yet females remain underrepresented in preclinical studies of Parkinson's disease (PD) and L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). We previously demonstrated that sub-anesthetic ketamine reduces established LID, attenuates dyskinesia development, and produces anti-parkinsonian effects in male unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) rat models. However, whether these therapeutic effects extend to females remained unknown. Here, we evaluated the anti-dyskinetic and anti-parkinsonian effects of sub-anesthetic ketamine in female Sprague-Dawley rats using the attenuation and established models of LID. In the attenuation paradigm, unilateral 6-OHDA-lesioned females received repeated L-DOPA administration with either ketamine (20 mg/kg, i.p.; 10-h dosing paradigm) or vehicle. Ketamine significantly attenuated the progressive development of dyskinesia, indicating that early intervention modified the trajectory of LID expression. In the established LID paradigm, ketamine produced robust significant acute reductions in abnormal involuntary movements (AIMs) after dyskinesia had fully developed, and these significant effects persisted for up to 49 days following treatment, demonstrating sustained suppression of dyskinesia severity. To determine whether ketamine altered therapeutic motor function, forelimb adjusting steps testing was performed in female unilateral 6-OHDA rats. Ketamine did not impair L-DOPA-mediated motor improvement suggesting compatibility with the gold standard medication. Ketamine was also by itself associated with significantly improved stepping performance during ketamine treatment conditions, indicating acute anti-parkinsonian motor benefit. Together, these findings demonstrate that the anti-dyskinetic and anti-parkinsonian effects of ketamine extend to female preclinical models and strengthen the translational rationale for repurposing sub-anesthetic ketamine as a potential therapeutic strategy for individuals with LID.

papers.title: Distinct medial septal GABAergic pathways differentially regulate spatial memory and network activity
papers.abstract: Septal GABAergic projection neurons form distinct pathways to subregions of the hippocampal formation, including the hippocampus proper and the medial and lateral entorhinal cortices. Parvalbumin (PV+) and calbindin expressing (CB+) projections target different types of interneurons and thereby differentially regulate neuronal activity in the downstream area. Consistent with the idea of dissociable functional roles, inhibition of septal PV+ neurons impairs reference memory whereas inhibition of septal CB+ neurons impairs both reference and working memory. Here, we show that these functions are differentially supported by specific projection pathways: PV+ projections to the dorsal hippocampus and medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) support reference memory, whereas CB+ projections to the MEC support both reference and working memory. At the network level, septal PV+, but not CB+, neurons regulate theta oscillations. Together, these findings further define the roles of septal PV+ and CB+ pathways in orchestrating network activity and supporting specific forms of memory.

papers.title: Multimodal characterization of putative pan-inhibitory viral constructs in macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: Transgenic approaches and validated viral vector toolboxes have advanced our understanding of how inhibitory neurons shape cognition and motor control in mice and other rodents. However, such advances have been elusive in non-human primates (NHPs). While many studies demonstrate expression of reporter proteins, few studies have provided clear quantitative evidence of whether these viral constructs can be reliably used for assessment of in vivo and in vitro function in primates, which, in turn, has hindered widespread adoption by NHP researchers. Here, we characterize putative pan-inhibitory cell targeting vectors engineered with regions from the Dlx5-6 intergenic domain. Pan-inhibitory viral vectors are attractive because they enable ground-truth optotagging and modulation of multiple inhibitory subtypes in the same animal and, when combined with machine learning approaches, enable cell-type classifiers for NHPs. We combined in vivo anesthetized electrophysiological recordings, in vitro slice electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry across seven rhesus macaque monkeys to assess the specificity, completeness and efficacy of three constructs in multiple sensory and higher-order association cortices. The vectors reliably restricted transgene expression to inhibitory neurons (81-97%). However, of the local GABAergic neurons only 32-64% expressed the transgene, depending on the construct. This incompleteness arose in part from uneven coverage across subtypes, with strong transgene expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons (~60-90%), sparse expression in calbindin-positive interneurons (~1-7%), and near-complete avoidance of calretinin-positive interneurons. A construct pairing DLX2.0 with ChrimsonR was excellent for in vivo optotagging, while h56D paired with bReaChES most effectively suppressed neural activity in vivo. In the slice, activating terminals of transgene-expressing neurons optically evoked inhibitory currents in coupled pyramidal neurons confirming transsynaptic functionality of these constructs and their use for inhibitory circuit-specific synaptic assessments and manipulation. Collectively, the results provide rigorous functional characterization, and quantitative guidance for NHP researchers seeking to deploy GABAergic cell-type-specific tools in their experiments.

papers.title: Cerebrovascular Structure-Flow Gradients Revealed by Volumetric Ultrasound Localization Microscopy
papers.abstract: Characterizing the joint organization of microscale cerebrovascular structure and flow in vivo is challenging. Volumetric ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) provides spatially resolved measures of microvascular structure and flow from the same acquisition, but how these features are jointly organized across brain networks remains unclear. Here, we characterized local vascular phenotypes from transcranial volumetric ULM in mice and examined whether they contained reproducible low-dimensional organization. Local measures of vascular structure and flow dynamics were summarized within corresponding brain regions across mice. Subject-specific vascular phenotype similarity matrices were combined into a group-consensus graph and analyzed using diffusion embedding. Two leading gradients, showing distinct spatial distributions across brain networks, were reproducibly recovered across subject and spatial scales. The principal gradient was associated with local vascular density and flow complexity, defining a vascular structure-related axis. The secondary gradient was associated with flow speed and acceleration, defining a flow-dynamics-related axis. These gradients provide a low-dimensional representation of the cerebrovascular structure and flow and provide a reference for studying coordinated vascular changes across disease, aging, and intervention.

papers.title: DPYD links glial lipids and myelination to sleep duration
papers.abstract: The regulation of sleep is heritable and conserved across species1,2, but the governing genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the role of DPYD--which encodes the pyrimidine catabolic enzyme, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase--in sleep. Using a cross-species approach, we show that DPYD and its orthologs act specifically in glia to promote sleep through the regulation of brain lipids. In mouse and zebrafish, we find that DPYD orthologs are enriched in oligodendrocyte lineage cells, and their loss reduces myelination and sleep independent of DPYDs established role in uracil catabolism to {beta}-alanine. Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of myelin in zebrafish show that altering myelination is sufficient to perturb sleep duration. In Drosophila, which lack myelin, we find that the DPYD ortholog acts in ensheathing glia to promote sleep through formation of glial lipid droplets, a proposed evolutionary precursor to myelin. Furthermore, a human GWAS-identified sleep variant2 resides in a conserved cis-regulatory element that selectively contacts the promoter of DPYD within oligodendrocytes, connecting the human genetic association to oligodendrocyte-specific control of DPYD. Together, these results identify a deeply conserved role for glial lipids in sleep regulation and establish DPYD as a mechanistic link between myelin biology and sleep.

papers.title: Serial dependence carries the action that produced the previous report
papers.abstract: Serial dependence pulls current judgments toward the recent past, but what is carried forward is debated: the previous stimulus, the previous decision, or something about the report itself. Three magnitude-reproduction experiments separated these sources. Participants viewed dot arrays that varied independently in duration and numerosity, then reproduced the cued dimension by holding a key while a display accumulated, so that both magnitudes were produced through the same action. A response-history model partitioned the attraction into previous-stimulus and previous-response paths. The previous response predicted cross-dimensional attraction after controlling for the previous and current stimuli: a numerosity report biased the next duration judgment and vice versa (Experiment 1), also when each task used its own response key (Experiment 2). A task switch weakened this carryover without abolishing it. Experiment 3 randomized, trial by trial, whether a reported number required a long or a short key hold. The influence of a previous number on the next duration judgment changed with this mapping, showing that reported value alone did not account for carryover. Conventional stimulus-based measures showed none of this cross-task history. Serial dependence can therefore carry the trace of the action through which a previous judgment was expressed, bounded but not gated by task context.

papers.title: Dyskinesia induced by a dopamine 2 receptor-like agonist, but not a dopamine 1 receptor-like agonist, is blocked by sub-anesthetic ketamine
papers.abstract: L-DOPA remains the most effective symptomatic treatment for Parkinson's disease, but chronic administration is frequently complicated by L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). Our prior work has established that sub-anesthetic ketamine can reduced LID acutely and has a long-lasting neuroplastic effect. This study tested whether low-dose ketamine reduces dyskinesia induced specifically by dopamine D2R-like or D1R-like receptor activation. Male Sprague Dawley rats were primed with daily L-DOPA to establish dyskinesia and then challenged with quinpirole, a D2R-like receptor agonist, or SKF-81297, a D1R-like receptor agonist, to induce abnormal involuntary movements (AIMs). After stable AIM baselines were established, animals received agonist plus vehicle or agonist plus ketamine. Limb, axial, and orolingual AIMs were scored on the acute treatment day (D0) and after washout on D4 and D7. Quinpirole and SKF-81297 reliably produced stable total LAO AIM scores following L-DOPA priming. Ketamine significantly reduced only quinpirole-induced, but not SKF-81297-induced, total AIMs compared with vehicle on D0, demonstrating an acute anti-dyskinetic effect. This reduction persisted after washout, with ketamine-treated animals continuing to show significantly lower AIMs on D4 and D7. Time-course analyses further showed reduced AIMs expression across the post-quinpirole observation period on D0 and at multiple time points on D7. These findings demonstrate that ketamine suppresses quinpirole-induced dyskinesia in L-DOPA-primed male rats and suggest that D2R-like receptor-mediated or indirect pathway-related mechanisms, but not direct pathway-related mechanisms, may contribute to ketamine's anti-dyskinetic effects. Together, these results extend prior work on ketamine by linking its sustained anti-dyskinetic effects to dyskinesia driven by D2R-like receptor stimulation in vivo.

papers.title: Reaction-time asymmetry covaries with shifts in hand choice in macaques
papers.abstract: How primates choose which hand to reach with remains poorly understood. Humans prefer the hand on the target's side of the body midline, and that preference shifts with biomechanical cost and with head and gaze direction. Earlier monkey studies used only two targets, one per side, too few to fit a psychometric function. Reaction time may also reflect the choice; in humans it is longest at the point of subjective equality (PSE), the target position at which either hand is equally likely to be chosen. We measured hand choice at ten horizontal target positions in two male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) that chose freely on each trial. For peripheral targets, both animals used the hand on the same side of the body midline, with a well-defined transition in between. Displacing the hands, rotating the head, or displacing gaze to one side each moved the PSE toward that side. Reaction time was longest near the PSE. Hand displacement slowed the hand on the displaced side, and gaze displacement slowed the hand opposite the gaze. In every condition, the farther the PSE lay toward one side, the slower that side's hand was relative to the other. Macaque hand choice thus resembles human hand choice, making the macaque a tractable model for studying how the brain chooses a hand.

papers.title: Predicting cortical signal mixing in coarse-resolution fMRI: a forward-operator analysis of surface mapping and the conditional benefit of correction
papers.abstract: Surface-based fMRI projection can mix signals from cortical locations that are close in the volume but distant along the folded cortical sheet. We constructed an anatomy- and acquisition-informed linear forward operator to estimate this mixing and evaluated a regularised surface reconstruction that inverts it. In HCP 7T geometry, the operator-predicted net far-cortex contribution to a standard surface value exceeded 5% in 4%, 10% and 22% of the group-average cortex at 1.6 mm and at emulated 2.4 and 3.2 mm resolution. Including the modelled far component improved predictions of emulated coarser maps and of real coarser StudyForrest sessions in high-leakage regions. Against finer-resolution, cross-run fMRI references, the regularised reconstruction reduced the residual error in HCP development data (n = 15) and in a pre-specified, family-independent confirmatory analysis (158 participants in 86 families). The improvement increased with a response-weighted contamination measure in HCP and in an independent 3T dataset (35 test participants), although a coarse-data-only version of the measure did not generalise to 3T, where an anatomical atlas predicted the gain at twofold coarsening. Overall performance improved at twofold, but not 1.5-fold, coarsening in the 3T sample. Ablation and data-reduction analyses were consistent with an important contribution from local deconvolution but did not uniquely identify the mechanism. Benefits were smaller or absent for multi-run averages, and no robust improvement across separately acquired sessions was established. The leakage maps characterise model-predicted, signed mixing rather than directly measured signal origins, and every gain is measured against an fMRI reference rather than against the true cortical response. Code, analysis plans and group leakage maps (7T and 3T) are provided in a public repository.

papers.title: Direction-Dependent Encoding of Forward and Inverse Models in the Same Purkinje Cells
papers.abstract: Saccadic eye movements are too fast to be guided by sensory feedback and therefore depend on precisely calibrated internal models. The cerebellum is widely thought to compute both forward and inverse models, yet how these two computations coexist in the same circuit remains unclear. We hypothesized that the same Purkinje cells (PCs) can serve as a forward model for saccades in one direction and as an inverse model for saccades in the opposite direction, because target neurons on either side of the cerebellar nuclei contribute differently to leftward and rightward saccades. To test this hypothesis, we recorded from PCs in the oculomotor vermis of macaque monkeys during repetitive saccade paradigms that induce adaptation and fatigue. Using the preferred error direction of each PC conveyed by increased complex spike (CS) activity (CS-on direction) as a proxy of the side of the cerebellar nuclei it projects to, we compared population activity for saccades directed against the CS-on direction (CS-on opposed) and along it (CS-on aligned). CS-on opposed saccades, (toward the PC's projection side) were accompanied by a precisely timed, sharp burst of simple spike (SS) activity at saccade onset that scaled with peak velocity, and CS error sensitivity was highest after the saccade. SS activity also changed systematically after adaptation, reflecting the altered kinematics of the adapted saccade. These properties are consistent with a forward model that estimates ongoing movement and updates itself based on post-movement error. In contrast, the CS-on aligned saccades, (away from the PC's projection side) were accompanied by broader SS modulation around saccade offset, and the CS error sensitivity was highest before the saccade. CSs around saccade onset encoded target location and initial eye position, and their occurrence was associated with reduced saccade amplitude. This reduction likely adjusts the motor command to the starting eye position, as expected for an inverse model that pre-programs the motor command before movement begins. Together, these findings provide neural evidence that the same PC population can contribute to both forward and inverse model computations, depending on saccade direction.

papers.title: PHASOR: An Open-Source Pipeline for Hidden Markov Model Analysis of Stimulus-Locked Retinal Multielectrode-Array Population Activity
papers.abstract: Multielectrode-array recordings of the retina reveal neural population activity at cellular resolution, but relating recurring population states to stimulus timing and single-unit responses requires several linked analysis steps. We present PHASOR (Population HMM Analysis of Stimulus-locked Output in the Retina), a pipeline that combines stimulus-clock alignment, Fourier-based response classification, hidden Markov modeling with Chow-Liu tree emissions, model-order selection, and state visualization. We evaluated the workflow with synthetic populations and demonstrated its use in ten ex vivo recordings from three wild-type retinas (two male, one female) and one male rd1 retina, including 2 Hz full-field sinusoidal stimulation. Across ten synthetic datasets containing seven generative states, selected model orders ranged from seven to nine, with a mean of 7.9, matching the generative count exactly in three of the ten datasets. A representative confusion matrix showed a near one-to-one correspondence between generative and decoded states, with a single additional low-occupancy state, illustrating the distinction between recovering temporal structure and recovering the exact state count. In a representative retinal recording, response classes differed in stimulus phase and contrast dependence, and decoded states differed in occupancy, dwell time, and active-unit composition. Recordings during L-AP4 application, without projected stimulation, and in a photoreceptor-degenerate rd1 retina illustrated changes in the resulting population-state descriptions. PHASOR integrates established analysis methods into a reusable workflow for relating stimulus-associated population activity to functional response classes. The selected states provide a descriptive model of population activity; their number and correspondence to biological assemblies require separate validation.

papers.title: Long term survival of chronically demyelinated axons in the taiep rat
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory demyelinating disease of the CNS in which neuroaxonal loss underlies permanent neurological disability. Axon loss in MS has been attributed to several causes, including loss of trophic/metabolic support from the myelin sheath. However, the contribution of chronic demyelination to axonal demise has been difficult to ascertain, due largely to the lack of long-lived models and uncertainty about the location of the primary injury site in long fibre tracts in MS patients. Here, we examine chronically demyelinated axons using light and electron microscopy of spinal cord tracts of 1- to 24-month-old taiep rats, in which the gene that is mutated, Tubb4a p.A302T, is expressed highly in oligodendrocytes. We find that small diameter axons in the dorsal column can survive for many months following demyelination. This is associated with significantly increased densities of oligodendroglia, and supernumerary glial cell processes. We hypothesise that trophic and metabolic support, sufficient to support axon survival, can be achieved through close contact between axons and glia. While efforts to restore myelin in MS remain crucial to recovering normal neurological function, myelin per se might not be a prerequisite for axonal survival under all circumstances.

papers.title: Sensory neurons gate a cortical plasticity window for immune encoding
papers.abstract: Activity-dependent plasticity allows brain circuits to encode experience, but this has been established with brief stimuli. Immune responses develop over days and are represented in the insular cortex (IC). How the cortex encodes experiences with this temporal structure is unknown. Here we show that Trpv1+ sensory neurons open a multi-day cortical plasticity window matched to the immune response. Following peripheral immune challenges, Parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons are activated first, restricting plasticity. Vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons respond two days later, disinhibiting IC excitatory neurons. Weaker challenges trigger the first phase but not the second, and preventing the transition blocks immune encoding, whereas lowering inhibition beforehand does not. These results identify a body-to-brain mechanism that gates cortical plasticity on the timescale of slowly evolving physiological experience.

papers.title: Systematic Spike Sorting Errors Revealed by Juxtacellular Ground Truth in the Awake Brain
papers.abstract: Existing ground-truth data for spike sorting come almost entirely from anesthetized or in vitro preparations. Yet phenomena expected to challenge spike sorting most (spike overlap and bursting) depend on brain state and differ in the awake brain. Therefore, error estimates from existing benchmarks may not transfer to awake recordings, and the types of errors in the awake brain remain largely uncharacterized. To address this, we generated a ground-truth dataset (16 neurons) using paired juxtacellular-extracellular electrophysiology in awake mice, and found spike sorting performance, particularly recall, to be lower than conventional benchmarks might suggest. Generally, false negatives sharply increased with intrinsic physiological factors like bursting, whereas false positives were more strongly associated with extrinsic factors, such as putative spike overlaps. To quantify contributions to errors from intrinsic and extrinsic factors, for each observed juxtacellular waveform we predicted the corresponding extracellular waveform. In the best-performing sorter, we estimate approximately half of false positives were attributable to credulous attempts to resolve putative overlaps. Bursting and putative overlaps were each associated with a roughly doubled false negative rate when they occurred separately, and with a sevenfold increase when they occurred together. These co-occurrences accounted for approximately 40% of a typical neuron's false negatives, despite comprising only approximately a fifth of its spikes. Thus, the moments when spike sorters must rely on the assumption of waveform invariance the most to resolve overlaps are exactly the moments when bursting makes that assumption least valid. We also estimate that three-quarters of false negatives had been detected but assigned to other units. These spikes were not cleanly oversplit: post-hoc merging was not productive because the loss in precision was three times the gain in recall. Because bursting and spike overlaps often co-occur, sorting spikes by waveform similarity and repairing the result by post hoc merging is unlikely to adequately balance precision and recall in the situations of greatest scientific interest. That is, while bursting and spike overlaps may involve only a minority of spikes, the resulting sorting errors may disproportionately distort the interpretation of neuronal population dynamics. We thus conclude that uncertainty quantification in sorters' output is essential.

papers.title: Donor Aware Reanalysis of Neuronal Nuclei Supports STMN2 Depletion Associated with Nuclear TDP 43 loss in FTD and ALS
papers.abstract: Background. Nuclear TDP-43 depletion is a central pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), but donor-to-donor variation can obscure transcriptomic associations in small postmortem cohorts. We reanalyzed public RNA-seq data from FACS-isolated NeuN-positive frontal-cortex neuronal nuclei to quantify gene-expression changes associated with nuclear TDP-43 loss while explicitly accounting for donor structure. Methods. The supplied GSE126542-derived matrix contained 62,754 genes across 12 libraries from seven donors, including five complete matched pairs. Source labels TDP-43 positive and TDP-43 negative were harmonized as nuclear TDP-43 retained and lost, respectively. After validation against featureCounts-assigned read counts, 44,225 genes with at least 10 total counts were analyzed using PyDESeq2. The primary model was ~ donor + nuclear_status; status-only and diagnosis-adjusted models were sensitivity analyses. The contrast was TDP-43 loss minus retained. Results. The donor-aware model identified 3,442 genes at false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05: 1,865 lower and 1,577 higher in TDP-43-loss nuclei. STMN2 was consistently depleted (log2 fold change = -1.813, 95% Wald interval -2.229 to -1.396; FDR = 6.22e-15), corresponding to approximately 71.5% lower expression. Normalized STMN2 counts were lower in TDP-43-loss nuclei in all five complete donor pairs. TARDBP expression was also lower (log2 fold change = -0.606; FDR = 4.98e-6). In contrast, UNC13A whole-gene expression was modestly higher in the donor-aware model (log2 fold change = 0.372; FDR = 0.00622) and was not significant in either sensitivity model. Conclusions. Donor-aware analysis supports a robust association between nuclear TDP-43 loss and STMN2 depletion in this neuronal-nuclei cohort, alongside extensive but model-dependent transcriptomic variation. Whole-gene UNC13A expression cannot be used to infer UNC13A cryptic-exon inclusion or functional UNC13A depletion. No splice-junction, percent-spliced-in, isoform, or protein measurements were available; mechanistic claims therefore require junction-level and experimental validation.

papers.title: Transplantation of human iPSC-derived retinal cells in the cone-dominant Northern tree shrew
papers.abstract: Abstract: Purpose: To characterize the transplantation and survival of photoreceptors generated from human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal organoids in the Northern tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri, TS). Methods: TS eyes were injected with retinal cells dissociated from GFP-expressing hiPSC-derived retinal organoids (12 animals; n=22 eyes). 15 eyes had prior damage induced by either experimental retinal detachment (n=11) or ATP-induced retinal damage (n=4), and seven eyes were undamaged. Retinal organoids were treated with Notch pathway inhibitor 2 days before transplant. TS retinal structure and cellular details were assessed post-transplantation for up to 8 weeks using scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and adaptive optics SLO (AOSLO). Histological analysis was done at the end of the experiment. Results: Cell transplants in eyes treated with a simple immunosuppression treatment failed to survive for more than 2 weeks (n=10 eyes). Robust cell survival was observed in the eyes treated with a complex immunosuppression cocktail for up to 8 weeks (n=12 eyes). The transplanted cells were confirmed to be subretinally located using OCT imaging and the cell fate was confirmed to be human photoreceptors by histology. Finally, AOSLO imaging captured structures resembling photoreceptor inner segments. Conclusions: Our results demonstrate survival of transplanted cells using a species-specific immunosuppression treatment. Future studies should aim to explore the long-term survival and function of the transplanted cells.

papers.title: Establishing an assay for visual desensitization in larval zebrafish for understanding synaptic plasticity
papers.abstract: Synaptic plasticity, the ability of neurons to modify the strength of their connections, is essential for learning. Desensitization is a type of synaptic plasticity during which a behavioral response to a stimulus is reduced after repeated presentations of a weakened version of the stimulus which does not produce the behavioral response and thus is deemed a subthreshold stimulus. Here we explore whether the larval zebrafish escape response from visual threats, such as an expanding dark spot, can act as a potential model to study desensitization. We developed a novel experimental setup to investigate visual desensitization, exposing larvae to looming visual threats of varying contrast, and used high-speed cameras to verify rapid escape movements. First, we established stimuli which reliably acted as subthreshold and suprathreshold stimuli. Next, we quantified the response rate before and after desensitization and compared those data to control larvae who were not desensitized. We observed desensitized larvae reduced their response rate to threatening looming stimuli. By providing an opportunity to explore the plasticity mechanisms governing sensory-motor transformations and behavioral adaptation, this research contributes to our understanding of fundamental principles of learning and neural plasticity across vertebrates.

papers.title: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell death does not contribute to lifelong population homeostasis
papers.abstract: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) proliferate and differentiate into myelinating oligodendrocytes throughout life, but it is unclear if their continuous self-renewal is balanced by cell death. We find that OPCs do not die during development or adulthood, nor during remyelination, acute systemic inflammation, or aging. These findings challenge the assumption that spontaneous OPC death is common and reveal that OPC homeostasis does not depend on programmed cell death.

papers.title: Integrated Characterization of Proximal and Distal Nerve Stumps in a Model of Chronic Motor Nerve Transection
papers.abstract: Prolonged peripheral nerve discontinuity subjects the proximal stump to chronic axotomy and the distal stump to chronic denervation, resulting in pathological changes that may compromise regeneration following delayed repair. Although these changes have been investigated in both nerve stumps, much of the existing evidence derives from mixed sensorimotor nerve models, leaving the histopathological changes of chronic motor nerve injury incompletely understood. Addressing this gap requires a well-defined, reproducible model that maintains prolonged motor nerve discontinuity and enables concurrent characterization of both nerve stumps. This study aimed to establish a chronic motor nerve transection model and characterize the distinct structural and microenvironmental changes occurring in both nerve stumps. The buccal branch of the facial nerve was transected in Lewis rats, and the nerve ends were secured to adjacent muscle to prevent spontaneous reconnection. At 10 weeks post-injury (p.i.), proximal and distal stumps were compared with uninjured nerves using histological, immunofluorescence, and morphometric analyses. Persistent functional impairment was observed throughout the study period. The proximal stump exhibited traumatic neuroma formation, altered axonal morphology, and loss of myelin integrity, but largely preserved its underlying nerve architecture and microenvironment. In contrast, the distal stump exhibited reduced neurofilament expression, clusters of small-caliber myelinated axons, and increased myelinated axon density compared to both uninjured nerves and the proximal chronically injured segment. These changes were accompanied by endoneurial tube atrophy, increased collagen I deposition, vascular remodeling, and immune-cell accumulation, indicating extensive structural and microenvironmental remodeling. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that chronic motor nerve transection produces two distinct pathological compartments: a proximal stump characterized by persistent but disorganized regeneration-associated features and a distal stump characterized by pronounced degenerative and microenvironmental changes. This study establishes a reproducible model of chronic peripheral nerve injury and provides a foundation for investigating how these compartment-specific pathologies contribute to regenerative failure and for developing targeted therapeutic strategies to improve regeneration following delayed nerve repair.

papers.title: Why probe registration is crucial for infant fNIRS and HD-DOT? An evaluation across 49 newborns
papers.abstract: Source-detector probe registration, i.e., the mapping of optode positions on the scalp to their true anatomical locations in head/brain space, is crucial for brain imaging with fNIRS or HD-DOT. While individual, MRI-based registration is desirable, it is not always feasible, motivating the development of alternative registration approaches. This study uses the STORM-Net registration protocol and quantifies the variation of cap alignment in a cohort of 49 newborns to evaluate how this affects reconstructed images using HD-DOT. Relative to a centrally aligned template, the cohort showed a median probe-position error of 10.12 mm, while the least and most misaligned subjects exhibited mean errors of 4.41 mm and 20.60 mm, respectively. The results demonstrate that the level of cap misalignment typically observed in newborn imaging can affect the spatial accuracy of reconstructed functional images, particularly in cases with larger probe displacements. These findings provide a quantitative basis for adopting more conservative interpretations of group-level functional brain activity and functional connectivity results, and strongly support the routine use of registration methods in infant HD-DOT studies.

papers.title: Photoentrainment as Bayesian Inference: How the central circadian clock may weight and integrate the intensity and wavelength of natural light to estimate astronomical time
papers.abstract: Synchronising with the Earth's 24-hour rotation using natural light as a timing cue presents a problem for the mammalian brain's central circadian clock. Natural light is highly variable and can take a range of values at any given time of day. For example, it fluctuates due to differences in weather conditions and across seasons. Therefore, an absolute value of light provides an uncertain indication of the time of day. Despite this uncertainty, the central clock maintains close alignment with astronomical time, and here we describe how this may be achieved computationally. We present a Bayesian model in which the clock's endogenous oscillation is used to predict the probability of observing features of light, including intensity and spectral composition, and their co-occurrence given the time of day. These predictions are drawn from a distribution of values typically experienced. When observed light falls outside the predicted range, a prediction error provides evidence that the clock may be misaligned with astronomical time. How much the clock adjusts its phase depends on the relative uncertainty associated with its internal prediction and observed light. These are combined as a weighted average according to their relative reliability, drawing the clock's updated phase towards whichever provides the more reliable estimate of astronomical time. Using natural light measurements collected over one week from 59 human observers and 100 days of environmental spectral measurements, we characterize how the variability of natural light systematically changes across the day and show how the clock may exploit this structure for circadian timekeeping. The model explains how the canonical shape of the phase response curve emerges from the relationship between light distributions and time of day, and how properties of light, including intensity and spectral composition, can be integrated according to their reliability. The central clock's synchrony to light may represent a specific instance of a general computational strategy employed by the mammalian nervous system, whereby sensory information is interpreted relative to an internally generated prediction.

papers.title: Circuit regulation along an activity continuum shapes flexible and stable representations during learning
papers.abstract: Learning requires neural representations to flexibly incorporate new information while progressively stabilizing to support enduring memories. How neural circuits balance these demands remains unclear. Here, we identify complementary mechanisms supporting representational flexibility and stability in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), a key component of the cognitive map for memory-guided navigation. Longitudinal calcium imaging in mice learning novel virtual environments revealed a persistent axis of excitatory neuronal activity associated with distinct representational dynamics. Low-activity neurons exhibited intermittent activation that varied with learning stages and greater learning-dependent representational refinement, flexibly shifting their encoding from landmarks toward reward locations. By contrast, high-activity neurons exhibited more persistent activation and maintained more stable spatial representations. Dopaminergic pre-reward ramping was associated with the emergence of reward encoding in low-activity neurons, whereas interactions with inhibitory interneurons contributed to the stability of high-activity neurons. Notably, interneurons exhibited activity changes opposing those of excitatory neurons during learning, and their transient activation upon novelty exposure delayed excitatory representational remodeling, stabilization, and behavioral learning, suggesting that inhibitory circuits gate learning-dependent representational dynamics. Together, these findings reveal how activity-dependent excitatory neuronal organization and circuit-level regulation enable complementary forms of representational flexibility and stability to coexist, facilitating the incorporation of novel experiences into stable, context-specific cognitive maps that support learning.

papers.title: BundleMorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-based Registration
papers.abstract: Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson's disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMorphometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.

papers.title: Multi-scale place fields provide a predictive basis for hierarchical control
papers.abstract: Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit unimodal spatial selectivity in small enclosures, but express multiple, irregularly spaced fields in environments of naturalistic scale. However, existing predictive-map theories of the hippocampus do not scale well to large environments and do not account for these heterogeneous place field characteristics. Here, we introduce the factorised hierarchical successor representation (fHSR), a predictive map that supports hierarchical control using subgoal-directed subroutines. We show that the fHSR allows efficient generalisation across tasks, scaling favourably with environmental size, and it reproduces key statistical and topological characteristics of multi-scale CA1 place cell activity in rats and bats. Analyses of experimental data further confirmed a novel prediction of the fHSR: population firing rates exhibit spatial periodicity with a characteristic wavelength independent of environmental size. These results identify the integration of hierarchical control and predictive representations as a normative principle that unifies efficient navigation with the spatial organisation of hippocampal activity.

papers.title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory
papers.abstract: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

papers.title: Dissociable norepinephrine and dopamine representations during strategic decision-making and reward learning
papers.abstract: Adaptive decision-making in competitive environments requires learning from immediate reward outcomes while tracking longer-timescale information to adjust behavioural strategies and remain unpredictable against others. Dopamine (DA) and norepinephrine (NE) have long been implicated in reward-guided behaviours, but their contributions to strategic choice remain unclear. We trained mice to play a zero-sum matching pennies game against a computer opponent that exploited regularities in their choice and reward history, such that optimal performance required stochastic choice decoupled from immediate reward. We combined fibre photometry recordings, behavioural and neural modelling, and a within-subject multi-task design to determine how NE and DA contribute to strategic choice in the matching pennies game versus reward-guided behaviour in a two-armed bandit (2AB) task. DA responses were dominated by trial-by-trial reward outcomes and consistently tracked model-derived reward prediction errors (RPE) across tasks and behavioural states. In contrast, NE activity reflected salient task events, predicted upcoming choice switches, and tracked longer-timescale variables including model-inferred behavioural strategy and average reward rate. In addition, NE responses were selectively enhanced following rewarded switches when these outcomes were informative for deciding whether to stay in or switch from the current strategy; and this enhancement could not be explained by RPE. Incorporating pre-choice NE activity into a reinforcement-learning model to modulate choice generation improved model prediction in matching pennies but not in the 2AB task. Together, these findings reveal complementary neuromodulatory correlates of competitive decision-making across timescales: DA primarily guides learning from immediate outcomes through RPE, whereas NE additionally represents contextual information and choice stochasticity relevant for shaping long-term strategies.
